One-sentence judgment: a Community Health Worker is not a volunteer handing out leaflets, but someone who promotes community health by helping individuals adopt healthy behaviors, advocates for individuals' health needs, and implements programs that promote, maintain, and improve the health of individuals and the community as a whole; O*NET defines this occupation as promoting community health by helping individuals adopt healthy behaviors; advocating for individuals' health needs by helping community residents communicate effectively with medical service providers or social service agencies; serving as a liaison or advocate and implementing programs that promote, maintain, and improve the health of individuals and the community as a whole; may provide health-related preventive services such as blood pressure, glaucoma, and hearing screenings; and may collect data to help identify community health needs; this page follows the O*NET-SOC 21-1094.00 precise occupational basis.

The work of a Community Health Worker can be divided into three connected but independent work surfaces. The first is health education and behavior support: advising clients or community groups on self-care (such as diabetes management); advising on improving overall health (such as diet or exercise); advising on risk or prevention (such as lead poisoning, human immunodeficiency virus, substance abuse during pregnancy, or domestic violence); advising on hygiene or cleanliness (such as flossing or handwashing); advising on diagnostic screening (such as breast cancer screening, Pap smears, glaucoma tests, or diabetes screening); advising on social or intellectual development (such as education, child care, or problem solving); teaching appropriate parenting behaviors to individuals or families; and teaching medical or oral health information to school groups, community groups, or specific families or individuals in a way consistent with cultural norms. The second is needs identification, referral, and advocacy: identifying the specific health care needs of individuals in a community or target area; referring community members to the health services they need; identifying or contacting high-risk or specific target groups (such as ethnic minorities, low-income groups, or pregnant women); developing plans or formal contracts to improve overall health for individuals, families, or community groups; advocating for individual or community health needs to government agencies or health service providers; giving feedback to health service providers on how to improve the accessibility or acceptability of services; assisting families in applying for social services (including Medicaid or the Women, Infants, and Children nutrition program); and providing interpretation, translation, or cultural mediation for community members regarding health services or information. The third is screening, home visits, records, and community liaison: conducting basic diagnostic procedures such as blood pressure screening, breast cancer screening, or infectious disease screening; administering immunizations or other basic preventive treatments; providing basic health services such as first aid; making home visits to pregnant women, newborns, or other high-risk individuals to monitor progress or assess needs; contacting clients in person, by phone, or in writing to confirm that they have completed the needed or recommended actions; monitoring the nutritional status of children, older adults, or other high-risk groups; maintaining client files containing plans, records, and related forms; collecting information from individuals to compile vital statistics on the overall health of community members; attending community meetings or health fairs to understand community issues or build relationships; distributing leaflets, brochures, or other information and educational materials to target community members; reporting suspected child or elder abuse, neglect, or threat of harm to the competent authority as required; and accompanying or transporting clients to scheduled health services or referral sites. The O*NET29 tasks with 14 Core and 15 Supplemental form an occupational task pool and are not all mandatory for every position; screening, immunization, and first aid tasks do not automatically confer clinical permission, and the occupational name or an overseas certification does not grant independent diagnostic and treatment authority; the specific procedures are verified per your own actual qualifications, jurisdiction, and institutional authorization.

First confirm the boundaries of the services and screening and immunization procedures your position allows; refer matters beyond that scope per procedure to personnel with the corresponding qualifications; do not write health education materials as individualized diagnosis, and do not substitute personal experience for medical advice.

Judgment three: whether mandatory reporting and confidentiality exception judgments are made per the legal requirements

The reporting obligation is verified per the jurisdiction, the person's status, the service user, and the triggering conditions. The current complete statutory text on child reporting was not obtained this round, so no uniform time limit or channel is specified here.
Judgment four: whether referral and resource linkage actually land and leave records

At referral, confirm service accessibility (eligibility conditions, cost, transportation, and timing), and follow up in person, by phone, or in writing to confirm that the service user has completed the corresponding action; when linkage is unsuccessful, record the barrier and help find alternative resources, rather than only issuing a referral slip.

Long-term exposure to difficult situations may bring emotional load; the following is an editorial self-check: verify team support, case handover, and rest arrangements, and do not independently take on tasks beyond your ability. paragraphs: The six directions share part of their abilities with this occupation: communication and listening, needs identification, records and follow-up, and awareness of privacy and boundaries. The real difference lies in the nature of the service and the qualification threshold: the management direction focuses on program and personnel coordination; the health and wellness coordination direction focuses on activity organization; the substance abuse and mental health counseling direction provides therapeutic services and requires clinical qualifications and supervision; the educational guidance and career counseling direction focuses on academic and career guidance; the social and human service assistant direction provides supportive services under supervision; and this occupation takes on health education, needs identification, referral and advocacy, and records and follow-up in community settings and does not provide clinical diagnosis or treatment. When choosing, it is suggested to first verify with a deliverable needs identification, education and referral plan, and record and follow-up exercise, rather than comparing names first.

The comparison basis is the occupational definition and task and work activity and work context description on the O*NET-SOC 21-1094.00 page, the related and adjacent occupation codes listed on that page, the adjacent occupation slug list registered by this evidence route, and the public occupational materials of each adjacent occupation; the comparison is an editorial summary and does not constitute a practice qualification, clinical advice, legal opinion, or public health conclusion.

values: Hypothetical task: using a hypothetical community health needs document and a set of hypothetical service recipient profiles, complete needs identification, health education key points, a referral and follow-up plan, and record key points.

Step one: write the needs identification and health education key points (list the verifiable needs items and the corresponding educational content, and point out which information in the given materials is insufficient to judge).

entries.answer:
Day-to-day work centers on health education and behavior support, needs identification and referral and advocacy, and screening and records and home visits and community liaison: advise clients or community groups on self-care and general health and risk prevention and hygiene and screening; identify the specific health care needs of individuals in a community or target area and refer community members to the services they need; develop plans or formal contracts with individuals and families and community groups to improve overall health; advocate to government agencies or health service providers about health needs and
feed back service accessibility; conduct basic screening such as blood pressure and infectious disease and carry out basic preventive procedures and first aid; make home visits to pregnant women and newborns or other high-risk individuals and monitor the nutrition of high-risk groups; maintain client files and contact clients in person or by phone or in writing to confirm that actions are completed; participate in community meetings and health fairs and distribute educational materials; and report suspected child or elder abuse and neglect and threat of harm to the competent authority as needed. The O*NET work context shows 98% 
maintaining continuous contact with others, 100% using email and phone every day, 69% considering dealing with the public extremely important, 90% on a regular schedule, and 63% working exactly 40 hours per week.
entries.question: What does a community health worker do every day?

entries.answer:
Social and community service managers coordinate programs and personnel and funding and usually do not take on frontline service and follow-up; fitness and wellness coordinators center on activity and program organization and do not do case referral; substance abuse and behavioral disorder counselors and mental health counselors provide therapeutic services and require clinical qualifications and supervision; educational guidance and career advisors focus on academic and career guidance; social and human service assistants provide supportive services under supervision; this occupation takes on health education and needs identification and
referral and advocacy and records and follow-up in community settings and does not provide clinical diagnosis or treatment. Shared abilities do not mean interchangeability: the nature of the service and the qualifications and responsibility boundaries differ.
entries.question: Where is the boundary between this occupation and adjacent occupations?

entries.answer:
You cannot infer that. The core tasks of this occupation include needs and risk judgment, interviewing and home visits and building trust, judging resource accessibility, applying mandated reporting and confidentiality exceptions, and driving resources to actually land; these steps depend on interpersonal judgment and institutional authorization and accountability. In addition, the ILO 
exposure index registered by this item's evidence route is only a task exposure measure, not a replacement rate or a job loss projection. The more reliable uses of tools are material translation and readability adjustment, and drafts of resource directories and records and statistics.
entries.question: Will AI replace community health workers?

entries.answer:
From the task structure, the earlier-affected parts are the structurable and digitizable steps: material translation and readability adjustment, organizing common questions, maintaining resource directories, organizing referral and follow-up records, and compiling statistics and archiving and reporting materials. The later-affected parts are the steps requiring judgment and relationships: needs and risk judgment, interviewing and home visits and building trust, judging resource accessibility, and applying mandated reporting and confidentiality exceptions and informed consent. It must be stressed that this judgment is an editorial summary, not an 
exposure measure or job projection provided by a source.
entries.question: Which tasks are most easily assisted?

entries.answer: Building trust in interviews and home visits and hearing what the other person really needs, judging priorities when resources are limited and driving resources to land, judging the applicability of mandated reporting and confidentiality exceptions, and maintaining professional boundaries and your own load over long-term accompaniment. These abilities depend on interpersonal judgment and institutional authorization; replacing any one of these steps with tool output would make 'who is responsible for the service recipient's privacy and safety' unanswerable.

description.text:
Community health workers help individuals in the community adopt healthy behaviors and serve as advocates and liaisons for their health needs, centering on health education and behavior support, needs identification and referral and advocacy, and screening and records and home visits: the 29 tasks and work context, the US wage and employment basis shown on the O*NET page (2025 wage and 2024—2034
